title: High Tech, Low Standards: High School in the Age of Distraction https://fordhaminstitute.org/national/research/high-tech-low-standards-high-school-age-distraction
author: Brian R. Fitzpatrick
source: Thomas B. Fordham Institute (fordhaminstitute.org), September 9, 2026, September 17, 2026
summary: This Fordham Institute report, authored by national research manager Brian Fitzpatrick with a foreword by Amber Northern and Michael Petrilli, draws on a nationally representative February to March 2026 survey of 1,011 current high school students and 1,013 recent graduates to examine technology use, AI, and grading as a single ecosystem. It reports four findings: 76 percent of respondents engage in at least one form of illicit tech use daily, much of it through school-issued devices on which YouTube, games, and shopping remain accessible; AI is widely used to bypass learning, including 26 percent who use it during quizzes or tests and majorities who believe homework has become meaningless; 62 percent spend most class time on school devices, which blurs sanctioned and unsanctioned work; and permissive grading (partial credit for missing work, routine retakes) combined with 57 percent reporting mostly A's makes distraction and AI misuse cheaper. The report's move is to argue these problems reinforce each other and to recommend device-time limits, in-class paper-and-pencil and oral exams, school-wide bans on routine retakes and no-penalty late work, working firewalls, and strict phone bans. The foreword adds that device-delivered teaching can reduce teachers to screen monitors and updates Sizer's Horace's Compromise for an era when students can check out without leaving the room.
points: Schools with phones locked in pouches or left in the office report 33 percent daily social media use versus 64 percent where policy is left to teachers, yet a third still use social media daily, so phone and school-device policies must be handled together.

Because 66 percent say YouTube is reachable on school devices and fewer than a third find firewalls easy to evade, much off-task use appears to stem from platforms that were never blocked rather than clever circumvention.
Respondents who spend three-quarters or more of class time on devices are more than twice as likely (35 versus 16 percent) to believe they could skip school without hurting their grades.
Among students scoring under 1000 on the SAT, 44 percent still report all or mostly A's, which the report reads as grade compression that makes high marks an unreliable signal of mastery.

The report recommends shifting weight to supervised in-class, paper-and-pencil and oral assessments, ideally externally anchored and blind-graded, with homework reoriented toward exam preparation where AI study aids become a reasonable use.
quotes: His findings show that school-issued devices are often misused, making them nearly as distracting as students’ personal cell phones. Combine that with unethical use of AI and rampant grade inflation, and we’ve sadly hollowed out the American high school experience.

In the hands of a less skilled instructor, technology can shift the teacher’s role from knowledgeable expert who sets high expectations and builds trusting relationships to a classroom monitor who watches students work on screens and tries to enforce on-task behavior.
Today, Horace’s students would have screens to help them sit quietly, making the compromise even easier. In other words, today’s kids can be sitting in class and still be somewhere else entirely.

Tellingly, analysis of survey metadata found that 22 percent of surveys completed by current students were filled out at least partially during typical school hours (between 9 a.m. and 2 p.m. local time on weekdays)—consistent with the patterns of off-task device use that the findings themselves document.

It also comes with a critical qualifier: even in schools with the strictest phone policies, nearly one in three respondents still reports daily social media use—likely via school-issued devices, personal laptops, smartwatches, or other devices not covered by phone bans. This underscores a key point: phone policies and school-issued device policies must be addressed together.
Unlike social media or gaming, which distract students from doing their work, AI tools can do the work for them—almost instantly, fluently, and in ways that are difficult to detect.
When most of the school day is organized around a screen, the dividing line between sanctioned academic work and unsanctioned browsing becomes invisible to the teacher.

If a student uses ChatGPT to prepare a study guide for an in-class exam on the Civil War, reviews it carefully, and then earns an A on the exam, that seems like a reasonable use of the tool. But if the same student uses AI during the exam to generate an essay or complete exam questions for them, the grade no longer reflects the student’s own understanding.
